title: Joshua 6:15–21
context: Joshua 6:15–21 narrates the seventh day. After the seventh circuit Joshua orders the shout and declares the city devoted (Hebrew herem) to the LORD. Rahab and her household alone are to live, and the precious metals go to the LORD’s treasury. Israel must not take anything that is devoted, or the camp will be brought under the curse (as happens with Achan in chapter 7). The wall falls, and the city and its people are destroyed. This is among the hardest texts in Scripture. Both traditions treat it as a unique act of divine judgment ordered by God at a particular point in redemptive history (Deuteronomy 7:1–5; 20:16–18; compare Genesis 15:16), not a pattern for later violence. Both also acknowledge that readers within each tradition explain its moral difficulty, its hyperbolic war language, and its relation to the rest of Joshua in different ways.

verses.text: On the seventh day, they rose early at the dawning of the day, and marched around the city in the same way seven times. On this day only they marched around the city seven times.
verses.arminianNotes: On the seventh day they rise at dawn and march around the city seven times, the only day they circle it more than once. Arminian readers see the climax of patient obedience, with the people faithfully carrying out the full command to the end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the seventh day as the completion God appointed. Some interpreters connect the pattern of seven with creation’s week, and the text does not develop that link explicitly. Both traditions read the day as the fulfillment of God’s word given in 6:2–5.

verses.text: At the seventh time, when the priests blew the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, “Shout, for the LORD has given you the city!
verses.arminianNotes: At the seventh circuit, as the priests blow the trumpets, Joshua tells the people to shout because the LORD has given them the city. Arminians emphasize that the victory is announced before the wall falls, so the shout expresses faith in what God has said.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that Joshua credits the victory entirely to the LORD’s giving. Both traditions see the shout as obedient faith answering God’s promise and read Hebrews 11:30 as confirming that the walls fell by faith.

verses.text: The city shall be devoted, even it and all that is in it, to the LORD. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, she and all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.
verses.arminianNotes: The city and everything in it are to be devoted (herem) to the LORD, except Rahab and those in her house, because she hid the messengers. Arminian readers see the exception as showing that God’s judgment is not blind: a Canaanite woman who turned to Israel’s God is spared, as her faith is later commended (Hebrews 11:31).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Rahab as a striking instance of God’s mercy within judgment, a Gentile brought into Israel and later named in Jesus’ genealogy (Matthew 1:5). Both traditions read the herem as God’s judgment on Canaanite sin (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5) and Rahab’s rescue as shared ground.

verses.text: But as for you, only keep yourselves from what is devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted it, you take of the devoted thing; so you would make the camp of Israel accursed and trouble it.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel must keep away from what is devoted, so as not to take any of it and bring the camp under the curse and trouble it. Arminians stress that the warning places a real responsibility on each Israelite, and chapter 7 shows that one man’s disobedience could bring trouble on the whole community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the corporate dimension: the sin of one member affects the covenant people. Both traditions read the verse as preparing for Achan’s sin in chapter 7, and both see what is devoted as belonging wholly to God, not to be taken for private gain.

verses.text: But all the silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD. They shall come into the LORD’s treasury.”
verses.arminianNotes: The silver, gold, and vessels of bronze and iron are holy to the LORD and go into his treasury. Arminian readers note that even the precious things of the city are not Israel’s spoil, which teaches that the conquest is not a war for plunder but an act carried out for God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the treasury as the place where the firstfruits of the conquest are given to God. Both traditions read the verse as consistent with the herem: Jericho, as the first city taken, belongs entirely to the LORD, whether by destruction or by dedication.

verses.text: So the people shouted and the priests blew the trumpets. When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight in front of him, and they took the city.
verses.arminianNotes: The people shout, the trumpets sound, the wall falls down flat, and Israel goes straight in and takes the city. Arminians read the account as plain miracle following trusting obedience, with God doing exactly what he promised in 6:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and stress that the wall falls by God’s power alone. Both traditions affirm the event as a real act of God in history. They recognize that the archaeology of Jericho is debated and that interpreters in both traditions weigh that evidence differently, without letting the debate replace the text’s own claim.

verses.text: They utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, both young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel utterly destroys everything in the city, man and woman, young and old, and the animals, with the sword. Arminian readers do not soften the verse. They read it as God’s specific judgment on Canaanite wickedness at a unique moment in redemptive history, not as a model for later wars, and they acknowledge the moral weight it carries for readers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as God’s righteous judgment on long-standing sin (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), commanded once and not repeatable by later believers. Both traditions also note that many interpreters in each discuss whether the language of total destruction includes stylized war rhetoric, and neither tradition speaks with one voice on that question.
